articles.title: Japan's English Proficiency Improves in Global Ranking
articles.intro: Explore a report on global English proficiency, Japan's progress, skill trends, age differences, and top-ranking countries in Asia and Europe.

sentences.text: Japan's English proficiency is improving, according to a new index — but it's still quite low compared to other countries.
English education company Education First (EF) has published the results of its English Proficiency Index, which looked at language proficiency in 117 countries.
This year's index includes data from 2.3 million people aged 18 and over.
Europe was once again the region with the highest English proficiency.
Sweden took first place in the global ranking, followed by Austria and Denmark.
However, globally, English proficiency got worse for the fifth consecutive year.
More than two-thirds of countries received lower scores than they did in 2025.
For example, the Netherlands — which ranked first for seven consecutive years — dropped to fifth place in this year's ranking.
Japan, on the other hand, saw an improvement.
It ranked 86th, up from 96th on last year's index.
It was the first time since the index was first released in 2011 that Japan has moved up in the rankings.
Japan's overall score also increased from 446 to 450, although this is still 35 points below the global average.
Of the four language skills tested, Japanese participants scored highest in reading, followed by listening, speaking and writing.
However, speaking and writing showed the biggest improvements compared with last year.
EF also found differences in English proficiency between age groups in Japan.
People aged 31 to 40 had the highest scores, while those aged 18 to 20 had the lowest.
The trend was also seen in many other countries, with younger adults tending to have lower English proficiency.
According to EF, one reason for this could be the COVID-19 pandemic.
Between 2019 and 2022, many young people had to take English classes online instead of in person, which could have affected their learning.
Malaysia ranked first in Asia, followed by the Philippines, Hong Kong, Nepal and South Korea.

articles.title: Scientists Grow Potatoes in Moon Soil
articles.intro: Learn about scientists growing potatoes in moon-like soil, compost’s role, and how this could help future astronauts live and grow food on the moon.

sentences.text: Boil 'em, mash 'em, eat 'em on ... the moon?
Full of nutrients, potatoes are a favorite here on Earth.
But they could perhaps help feed astronauts living on the moon one day.
Scientists in the US have now taken a step toward making that possible by growing potatoes in special soil made to be similar to the soil on the moon.
This could help astronauts grow their own food if people live on the moon in the future.
But growing potatoes in moon soil isn't easy.
Unlike Earth's soil, moon soil has very little organic material, which plants need to grow well.
So researchers at Oregon State University wanted to find out if adding compost could help.
Compost is made from old plants and other natural waste, and it has the nutrients that help plants grow.
The researchers used compost made with the help of earthworms.
They mixed different amounts of it into the moon-like soil and planted potatoes.
And the results were encouraging.
Potato plants grown in soil with 30% compost grew just as well as potato plants grown in normal Earth soil.
However, without compost, the potato plants were much smaller and had weak roots.
Adding smaller amounts of compost helped, but the plants still didn't grow as well as those grown with 30% compost.
The potatoes were also found to be safe to eat.
NASA hopes to have people living and working on the moon by the early 2030s, and growing food there could mean fewer supplies need to come from Earth.
Astronauts could take a small amount of compost to the moon, and make more using leftover food and plants.
This may be one small step for potatoes, but it's one giant leap for humans being able to live away from the Earth!

articles.title: Switching Dairy for Plants Risks Nutrient Deficiencies
articles.intro: This lesson covers the risks of nutrient deficiencies when replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives, based on new research findings.

sentences.text: There are many benefits to changing to a plant-based diet.

It can support health by offering a lot of fiber, vitamins and most essential nutrients, while also being more climate-friendly, because growing plant-based food is more sustainable than meat production.
However, changing to a completely plant-based diet still needs to be done carefully.
And a study has found that replacing dairy with unfortified plant-based products could lead to deficiencies in some essential nutrients.
The study was published in _Planetary Health_, and used data from around 3,000 people aged 18 months to 100 years.
They were all participants in the UK's National Diet and Nutrition Survey, which included four days of reports on what participants ate.

The researchers modeled what would happen if participants replaced the dairy in their diets with plant-based products, calculating the nutritional value of the dairy-free options using product labels and brand websites.
In particular, they looked at essential nutrients found in dairy products — calcium, vitamin B12, riboflavin and iodine.
We need calcium to build bones, and vitamin B12 to make red blood cells.
Riboflavin keeps our skin, eyes and nervous system healthy, while {{prn:iodine|io-dine}} is needed for the production of important hormones.

The researchers calculated that replacing dairy products with unfortified plant-based options reduced intake of each nutrient — and the effect was strongest among young children, teenagers and adult women.
{{prn:Iodine|i-o-dine}} was a particular problem.
For most people, replacing 50% of dairy with plant-based products led to a 13% to 28% decrease in iodine intake, for example.
And if teenagers replaced 100% of their dairy with plant-based products, 72% of boys would not be getting enough iodine — and neither would 80% of girls.

Instead of using the findings to say people shouldn't switch to plant-based foods, however, the researchers are calling for dairy replacements and other foods — like bread — to be fortified with nutrients like iodine that are hard to get without dairy.

articles.title: South Korea's Noodle Giants Fight for Global Sales
articles.intro: Explore how South Korea's top noodle brands, NongShim and Samyang, compete for global markets and evolve their products to boost international sales.

sentences.text: Two major South Korean food companies, which have long been rivals in their home country, are now fighting for global sales as Korean food becomes more popular overseas.
The companies NongShim and Samyang are both famous for their noodles in South Korea.
Founded in 1961, Samyang became the first South Korean company to sell instant ramen noodles in 1963.
But NongShim, founded in 1965, became the country's top instant noodle maker in 1991, and has controlled around 55% of the South Korean market since then.
These days, the two companies' signature brands are quite different.
NongShim is famous for its Shin Ramyun: noodles that come with a spicy beef soup and dried vegetables.
Samyang, on the other hand, is famous for its Buldak, which means "fire chicken" in Korean.
These stir-fried, soupless noodles in chicken sauce are much spicier than Shin Ramyun noodles.

In fact, Buldak noodles have won attention for their extreme spiciness, with videos of people trying the "fire noodle challenge" — eating Buldak noodles as fast as possible — going viral on social media.
Videos like these have helped increase Samyang's global popularity, and international sales now make up 80% of the company's total revenue.
Samyang has already overtaken NongShim in markets like China and Europe, and is close behind it in the US.
NongShim's international sales make up just 37% of revenue.
Now NongShim is trying to catch up with Samyang's success abroad by building a factory in Busan that will produce Shin Ramyun noodles for export to Japan, Europe, Australia, India and Southeast Asia.
NongShim believes the factory will boost its export capacity by 70%.
By 2030, NongShim wants to double its global noodle sales to 5.4 trillion won, or about $4 billion, which would raise international sales to over 60% of its revenue.
NongShim has also clearly studied Samyang's success with soupless noodles, and it plans to bring out its own stir-fried Shin Ramyun next year.

articles.title: How Locals Help Japan's Lighthouses Attract Tourists
articles.intro: Learn how local groups in Japan are helping to preserve lighthouses and turn them into tourist attractions with tours, events, and educational visits.

sentences.text: For many years, they looked over the seas and helped guide ships to safety and welcome them home.
Now, some lighthouses in Japan are welcoming tourists instead!
There are about {{prn:3,100 | three thousand and one hundred}} lighthouses in Japan, according to _Kyodo News_.
However, some of these lighthouses are no longer in use.
In 2021, the Japan Coast Guard came up with a plan to look after these lighthouses and turn them into places tourists and residents could enjoy.
Under the plan, local groups help take care of the lighthouses, and also organize tours and events to bring in visitors.
So far, 62 organizations across Japan have joined the initiative, looking after 68 lighthouses.
For example, an organization in Toyama prefecture opens Ikujihana Lighthouse to visitors once a month between June and October.
People can enjoy beautiful views of the sea and nearby mountains from the lighthouse.
Another lighthouse, in Aichi prefecture, has become a popular place for school trips.
Children can learn about its history, walk around inside and even try turning on its light!
"We want people to learn about the history of lighthouses and the role they've long played in keeping ships safe," a member of the coast guard told _Kyodo News_.
Other countries are also finding ways to give old lighthouses a new life.
Visitors to the Harlingen Lighthouse in the Netherlands, for example, can actually sleep there!

articles.title: Think You're a Perfectionist? You're Probably Right!
articles.intro: Explore what it means to be a perfectionist, including research on self-identified perfectionism, its benefits, and its potential drawbacks.

sentences.text: Young adults who describe themselves as "perfectionists" are usually right about themselves.
That's what a study published in _Current Psychology_ found after working with about {{prn:990 | nine hundred and ninety}} young adults aged 18 to 25 living in the US.
The participants answered online surveys that asked if they identified themselves as perfectionists, as well as a number of questions designed to measure the traits linked with perfectionism.

Danielle Sirianni Molnar from Canada's Brock University explained that she and other researchers wanted to know if young people just called themselves perfectionists because it's seen as a good thing to be.

She gave the example of people saying they're perfectionists when asked to name a weakness during a job interview, knowing that it will still be seen as a positive even if it's presented as self-criticism.
While having high standards for yourself and your work has lots of benefits, there really are some problems that come with perfectionism.
It can be linked with low self-esteem, rigid "all-or-nothing" thinking, and a fear of failing.
The survey used three separate scales to measure perfectionism.
One scale looked at things like worries over mistakes, setting high personal standards, and experiences with parental expectations and criticism, as well as self-doubt and organizational skills.

The second scale was about having excessively high and rigid expectations, demanding perfection from other people, and thinking people demand perfection from you — which can result in high levels of self-criticism.
The final scale looked at the difference between perfectionism and "excellencism," which also means having and working to high standards, but in a more reasonable, flexible way.
The study found that participants who self-identified as perfectionists scored highly for perfectionism across all three of these scales.
This suggests that not only are they really perfectionists, but they have an accurate view of themselves and what that means!

articles.title: Japan Considers New Tax on Electric Cars from 2028
articles.intro: This lesson explores Japan's proposal for a new tax on electric vehicles, its reasons, potential effects, and the growth of electric car sales.

sentences.text: The Japanese government is looking at introducing a new tax on electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids starting in May 2028, according to _Kyodo News_.
The tax would be added to the vehicle weight tax that drivers already pay during regular car inspections.
The amount would depend on the car's weight, and people with plug-in hybrids would likely pay about half as much as those with all-electric vehicles.
Only about 3% of cars sold in Japan are electric, while in China that number is around 33%, and in Europe it's 22%.
So why introduce a new tax on these vehicles?
The goal is to make sure all drivers help cover the cost of maintaining roads.
Drivers of gasoline cars already help pay for this through taxes on gas, while those with electric cars use the same roads without paying these taxes.
Electric cars are also often heavier than similar gasoline cars because of their large batteries, meaning they cause more damage to roads.
The government has yet to decide how much the new tax will be.
However, automakers have called for a delay, saying that the tax could make Japanese drivers even less likely to choose an electric car.
However, there are signs that more people in Japan are interested in buying electric cars.

On November 20, for example, the government closed applications for subsidies for electric and other environmentally friendly vehicles because sales were higher than predicted and money was running low, according to _Kyodo News_.
Plans for next year's subsidies are yet to be decided.

articles.title: Americans Are Stressed and Asking AI for Help
articles.intro: Explore why many Americans feel ongoing stress, its main causes, and the growing trend of turning to AI for advice and emotional support.

sentences.text: Nearly three-quarters of US adults think stress is unavoidable, and something that they just have to "live with."
And to make that stress easier to manage, many are asking AI for support.
This is what was found in the _2026 Stress in America_ survey from the American Psychological Association (APA).
The survey, which included over 3,000 US adults, asked people about their main causes of stress — and it's likely no surprise that money worries topped the list.

Seventy-seven percent of participants said that dealing with the cost of living — including keeping up with their house payments or rent, and paying for groceries — was a significant source of stress in their lives.
Around three-quarters of Americans also said that worries about the future of their country were a big source of stress.
And stress is changing how Americans are living their lives.
Almost half of survey participants said they have avoided social events in the past year because of stress, uncertainty or feeling overwhelmed.
Many are looking to AI for help.
Forty-nine percent said they have talked to AI like it was a friend, while 47% said they have used AI like a mental health professional.
One in 10 said they actually rely on AI more than friends and family for advice.
If stress is truly unavoidable, that may sound like a cheap and easy way to deal with it.
But the APA's Arthur C. Evans Jr. isn't so sure.
"Chronic stress can take a serious toll on people's physical and psychological well-being," he said.
But he also added, "We should not accept that toll as an inevitable part of everyday life."

He also warned against relying on AI for support, saying that while it might help, it cannot replace trained mental health professionals or the human connection that comes from relationships with family and friends.

articles.title: US Data Centers Use as Much Energy as Some Countries
articles.intro: This lesson explores how US data centers use vast amounts of energy, their link to AI growth, and their significant environmental impact.

sentences.text: The largest US data centers are collectively using as much energy as some countries, according to a new study.
The largest data centers, which are used mainly to support the development of AI, are known as "hyperscale data centers," or HDCs.
And America's fast-growing number of HDCs has led to worries about carbon dioxide emissions.
Researchers in the US and Italy looked at data from 403 HDCs operating in the US between May 2024 and April 2025.
They estimated these HDCs' electricity consumption, how that electricity was generated, and the carbon dioxide emissions that would be created as a result.
They estimated that these HDCs consumed 82 terawatt-hours of electricity — which amounts to 1.8% of all the electricity used in the US during the period studied.

The researchers also estimated that around 54% of the electricity used by these HDCs came from fossil fuels, and that they were responsible for the emission of nearly 26 million metric tons of carbon dioxide.
That's about the same as the annual carbon emissions of Denmark, a country of 6 million people.

Gianluca Guidi, the lead author of the study, told _CBS News_ that the research team's estimates were actually likely to be low — because since the end of their study period in April 2025, the number of HDCs in the US has more than doubled.
"The industry is growing faster than anyone can track it," Guidi said.
The tens of thousands of computers inside HDCs create lots of heat, and need constant cooling as they run 24 hours a day.
Much of the extra energy they need comes from new gas-fired power, which developers sometimes even build on-site rather than opting for renewable power.
But Guidi says there are better ways to power AI.
"We've proven we can build AI really fast.
Now, let's prove that we can build it right," he said.

articles.title: Many US Teens Are Better with Money than Parents
articles.intro: This lesson explores a survey showing US teens excel at managing, earning, and saving money, sometimes outperforming their parents financially.

sentences.text: Teenagers often have a reputation for spending money as soon as they get it.
But a new survey suggests that many teenagers may actually be better at managing money than their parents — in the US, at least.
The survey, done by Talker Research, asked parents and teenagers aged 13 to 17 about money habits.
It found that almost half of parents believe their teenagers understand money better than they do.
And 90% of teenagers also said they're good at managing money!
Most of the teenagers surveyed are already earning their own money.
Some get paid for doing jobs around the house, while others have part-time jobs or have found other ways to make money.
On average, they earn almost $7,000 a year.
And rather than spending it all, they save nearly half of it.
In fact, 36% of parents said their teenager saves more than they do!
Some parents said their children think more carefully than they do before buying expensive things, and are better at waiting and saving up for something they want.
And it's not just about saving money.
About one-third of parents said their teenagers are better at sticking to a budget, knowing the difference between things they want and things they need, and being careful about borrowing money.
Some parents even said their teenagers are better at finding ways to earn extra money and have clearer plans for their financial future.
When asked what they think their lives will look like in 10 years, some teenagers talked about having good jobs, starting businesses or earning enough to support their families.
Not all teenagers have the same dreams, of course.
But many seem to be taking money seriously — and their parents might be able to learn a thing or two from them!

articles.title: Why Small Acts of Kindness Can Make a Difference
articles.intro: Explore how small acts of kindness and fleeting interactions with strangers can have a powerful, positive impact on people's lives and connections.

sentences.text: You're shopping at a supermarket and see a mother with a young child who keeps crying.
The mother looks tired and embarrassed, and she doesn't know what to do.
But then a stranger smiles at her and says, "Don't worry.
You're doing a great job."
It's a small moment.
But a researcher at the University of Georgia believes that small interactions with strangers can be more important than we think.
Joseph Hermanowicz has studied how small acts of kindness can help people feel connected to others.
He calls these moments "evanescent interactions."
They're more than just being polite to people — for example, just saying "good morning" or holding open a door for someone — because these interactions make people feel noticed and understood.
We don't usually think strangers will notice how we're feeling, or that they might offer support.
That's why these unexpected moments of kindness can mean so much.
And the positive feelings can go both ways.
Both people may feel a connection, even if they never meet again.
Hermanowicz first noticed how important these connections are while studying why some students leave college before finishing their studies.
He spoke with students who had left college, and found that some felt alone and unnoticed.
Some said that even a short, friendly conversation might have helped them feel that they belonged.

Stories like these led Hermanowicz to start thinking about the importance of these "evanescent interactions," and why small acts of kindness may be especially important for people who feel lonely or disconnected from others.
He also says the good feelings don't always end when the interactions are over — remembering these moments later can bring those feelings back.
So the next time you see someone having a difficult day, remember that a smile or a few kind words could make a real difference!

articles.title: Japan Comes Last in Global Workplace Happiness
articles.intro: Explore a global survey on workplace happiness, focusing on why Japan ranks last and what factors influence employee joy and engagement worldwide.

sentences.text: What makes people happy at work?
Is it being interested in what they do?
Having friendly colleagues?
Feeling that their boss values them?
A new international survey has looked at how happy people are at work.
The survey, by French employee benefits company Edenred, asked about 26,000 people in 27 countries about their experiences at work.
It looked at things like people's relationships with colleagues, their feelings about their jobs, and whether they felt valued for what they did to find their "joy score."
The average "joy score" for all 27 countries was 63 out of 100.
India had the highest score, at 73.
Mexico and Peru were close behind, with 72 points each.
But Japan came last, with just 47 points out of 100.
In fact, more than half of the Japanese workers in the survey fell into the "low joy" group.
The survey also found that 40% of Japan's human resources managers believed that worker engagement had improved over the last year — but only 10% of workers said they actually felt more engaged.
Around the world, 94% of workers in the "high joy" group said they expected to stay with their company the next year.
For the "low joy" group, it was 63%.
This doesn't mean that happiness makes people stay in their jobs.
But the two seem to be connected.
So what helps people feel happier at work?
The survey found that workers who received recognition or praise from their bosses were more likely to want to stay with their company.
So for companies that want to keep their workers, saying "thank you" for a job well done could be a good place to start!

articles.title: South Korea to Survey Young K-Pop Stars on Rights
articles.intro: Explore concerns over young K-pop stars' rights, training conditions, and government plans to survey and protect underage performers in South Korea.

sentences.text: K-pop has become one of South Korea's most successful cultural exports, with groups like BTS, Blackpink, Stray Kids and Babymonster finding fans around the world.
Their slick choreography and highly polished performances are hard work, though.
Would-be stars have to do intense training, often starting at a young age.
The South Korean government has now announced plans to survey underage performers on their contracts after a _New York Times_ report prompted concerns over the rights of young K-pop stars.

South Korea's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism plans to do the survey in 2027, with the goal of examining whether existing rules do enough to protect underage performers' rights to education and rest.
It aims to find out exactly how many underage artists are currently represented by entertainment agencies in South Korea, their ages, and if their basic rights are being respected.
Concern about the safety of young performers is nothing new, and the country actually passed a range of laws in 2014 aimed at protecting their rights and limiting their work hours.

However, in November of this year, investigators from _The New York Times_ reported that members of the group NewJeans had signed contracts with record label Ador when they were aged 14 to 17 that effectively waived their rights to "sleep, rest and free choice."
The report also raised concerns about the members being required to cover a portion of the expenses for their training, as well as cosmetic surgery and dermatological treatments.
Ador is owned by Hybe, which represents BTS.
Hybe told _The New York Times_ in a statement that the company follows child-protection laws, and works hard to protect its entertainers.
However, the investigation also revealed that the contracts signed by NewJeans were missing standard child protection language.
NewJeans actually tried to leave Ador in November 2024.
But almost a year later, the Seoul Central District Court declared that they still had to honor their contracts, which expire in 2029.
Soon after, one of the five members was fired and sued for 33 billion won — about $25 million.

articles.title: Americans' Thanksgiving Dinner Is Getting More Expensive
articles.intro: This lesson explores the rising cost of Thanksgiving dinner in the US, highlighting price changes for ingredients and reasons behind the increases.

sentences.text: From delectable roast turkey to cranberry sauce and sweet potatoes, Thanksgiving in the US wouldn't be complete without a hearty meal shared with family and friends.
But putting that meal on the table is putting a bigger hole in people's wallets.
The American Farm Bureau Federation's annual Thanksgiving dinner survey found that a meal for 10 people costs about $59 this year.
That's an increase of more than 6% from 2025.
This is the first time since 2022 that the survey has recorded an increase in the cost of a Thanksgiving dinner.
The price of turkey has seen one of the biggest increases.
A frozen turkey weighing about 7.3 kilograms now costs an average of about $24, an increase of 10% from last year.
The cost of cranberries has increased by nearly 9%.
Other ingredients like milk, bread rolls, stuffing mix and sweet potatoes have also increased in price.
The Farm Bureau said high fuel prices and a shortage of farm workers have affected food production costs.
However, not everything has become more expensive.
Frozen peas, frozen pie crusts and whipping cream all cost less than they did last year.
That's good news for people who like pumpkin pie, a classic Thanksgiving dessert.
The survey also shows how Thanksgiving meal prices have changed over time.
In 2020, a dinner for 10 cost just under {{prn:$47|forty seven dollars}}.
Prices reached a record high of more than $64 in 2022 before falling again in subsequent years.
So although it's more expensive this year than it was last year, the cost of a Thanksgiving dinner is actually still 8% lower than it was four years ago.
American Thanksgiving is held on the fourth Thursday in November.
This year, that makes it November 26.
The Thanksgiving dinner survey has been done every year since 1986.
Hundreds of volunteer shoppers across all 50 US states and Puerto Rico take part by checking the prices of ingredients at local grocery stores.

articles.title: Japan Plans to Make It Easier to Become a Teacher
articles.intro: This lesson covers Japan's plan to ease requirements for becoming a teacher in response to a nationwide shortage of teaching staff.

sentences.text: Japan is planning to make it easier for working adults, or students who majored in another subject, to switch to a career in teaching.
A government education panel released a proposal on November 17 to make teaching licenses easier to get.
The goal is to encourage more people to enter a profession that is struggling to find enough staff.
One change would make it easier for university students to qualify.
At the moment, those preparing to teach in elementary, junior high or high schools must earn 59 credits in teaching-related subjects.
Under the new plan, this would fall to 36 or 37 credits.
Students would still need another 20 credits, but these could come from subjects they are already studying for their degree.
This would make it easier for students from different fields to become teachers.
The proposal would also include a one-year graduate course for working adults who hold a university degree or higher.
They would learn about teaching and spend time working in schools, where they would also receive compensation.
The plan comes as schools across Japan struggle to find enough workers.
According to an education ministry survey, more than 2,800 public schools in Japan started the 2025 academic year without enough teachers.
And fewer people are choosing teaching jobs.
In 2025, there were just 2.9 people applying for every teaching job, down from 3.2 a year earlier.
That was the lowest number on record.
The panel plans to finalize its recommendations by the end of 2026, with changes to the law expected to be proposed in 2027.

articles.intro: Explore TimeOut's list of the world's 28 coolest streets, featuring hotspots for food, art, and culture in cities across the globe.

sentences.text: What makes a part of a city "cool"?
Is it clubs?
Cafes?
Unique local shops?
_TimeOut_ has released its list of the world's 28 "coolest" streets for 2026.
And according to the magazine, a "cool" street is a place where people "want to spend their time right now."
That means these streets are "home to some of the very best places to eat, drink, dance, shop and hang out" in each city.
The magazine asked its editors and local experts for their ideas, and they decided that the coolest street in the world for 2026 is Song Wat Road in Bangkok, Thailand.
This {{prn:1,200-meter-long|one thousand and two hundred meter long}} street was once an important trade hub between Bangkok's Chinatown and the Chao Phraya River.
But these days, its old brick warehouses are full of restaurants, colorful street art, independent fashion stores and more!
In second place is London's Golborne Road.
It's known for its mix of Portuguese, Moroccan and Middle Eastern restaurants, as well as bars, cafes and vintage clothing shops.
In third place is Fernández de Enciso in Buenos Aires, Argentina.
This street has lots of cafes and restaurants where visitors can sit outside and eat under the trees.
Nearby Plaza Arenales is also a popular meeting place, where there are often events and live music.
Four of _TimeOut'_s 10 coolest streets are in Asia, with Singapore's Neil Road at number five, Hong Kong's Upper Lascar Row at number seven, and Beach Street in George Town, Malaysia, at number nine.
There are also two Japanese streets on the list.
Sanjo-dori in Kyoto is in 13th place.
It's known for its old red-brick buildings, many of which are now cafes, galleries and shops.
Oyafuko Street in Fukuoka is number 25.
_TimeOut_ said its list shows the "variety of street life" around the world.

articles.title: Okinawa Celebrates Restoration of Shuri Castle
articles.intro: Learn about the restoration of Shuri Castle in Okinawa, its history, cultural significance, and impact after a devastating fire.

sentences.text: Officials and residents in Okinawa celebrated the restoration of Shuri Castle's main hall on November 22, seven years after it was destroyed in a fire.
The building, famous for its deep red color and dragon decorations, is an important symbol of Okinawa's cultural heritage.
The fire broke out on October 31, 2019 during a festival at the castle complex in Naha, Okinawa's capital.
Firefighters struggled for nearly 12 hours to contain the blaze as it spread in strong winds.
The fire destroyed the main hall, two halls next to it and four nearby structures, while two other structures were heavily damaged.
Investigators could not determine the cause but considered an electrical fault the likeliest explanation.
"The fire was a tremendous shock to the Okinawan people," Okinawa Governor Genta Koja said at the restoration ceremony.
Shuri Castle dates back to the Ryukyu Kingdom, which ruled Okinawa for about 450 years until Japan took control in 1879.
The castle also represents Okinawa's recovery from World War II.
It was destroyed during the Battle of Okinawa in 1945, which killed about 200,000 people, including many civilians.
The castle was largely rebuilt in 1992, but work on some sections was still underway when the 2019 fire occurred.
For the latest restoration, experts used historical documents and new research to make the main hall more closely resemble the original building.
They even recreated its distinctive deep red color using a pigment made partly from iron bacteria found in northern Okinawa.
The main hall reopened to the public on November 23, while restoration of other buildings will continue in stages.
Experts say completing the entire castle could take more than a decade.
Shuri Castle is a major tourist attraction, and its restoration is expected to boost Okinawa's economy.
Koja, who took office in September, has promised to double the island's per capita income and tourism revenue within a decade and make it more attractive to young people.

articles.title: Study Shows Where in Lungs Vapes' Toxic Metals Go
articles.intro: Explore research on how toxic metals from vaping accumulate in different parts of the lungs and their potential health risks.

sentences.text: According to the World Health Organization, more than 100 million people around the world — including at least 15 million children — use e-cigarettes.
E-cigarettes and vaping are often marketed as a safer alternative to cigarettes.
However, not only do they still contain addictive nicotine, but research has found that they may leave toxic metals in users' lungs.
Some of these metals are in the liquid used to give e-cigarettes their flavor, but some also come from the heating elements that turn those liquids into a vapor.
In a study in _Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry_, researchers exposed mice to e-cigarette vapor twice a day over four days to better understand how metal builds up in a user's lungs.
The mice were divided into three groups, receiving the equivalent of eight, 16 or 32 vaping puffs in each session.
A fourth group only breathed normal air.
The device the researchers used to produce the vapor had a nickel-chromium heating element.
They used a commercially available vape liquid, which they analyzed and found also contained those two metals, as well as zinc, aluminum, copper, lead, mercury and more.
After four days of breathing the vapor, the researchers examined the mice's lungs, using a laser-based imaging system to map exactly where the metals had settled.
They found that different metals tended to build up in different places.
Lead and nickel settled more in the upper area of the lungs, as well as in the outer lining.
Zinc was found in higher concentrations at the bottom of the lungs.
There was evidence of metal in the lungs of all the mice that were exposed to the vapor.
For mice in the 32-puffs group, lead concentrations were 25 times higher than among the mice that just breathed normal air.
Many of the metals left by vaping are linked to health risks.
For example, nickel may damage the cells lining the airways.
And lead can be absorbed into the bloodstream, spreading to bones, the brain and other organs, where it may contribute to high blood pressure and cognitive problems.

articles.title: Jensen Huang Reinstated as Nvidia CEO
articles.intro: This lesson covers Jensen Huang’s resignation and swift return as Nvidia CEO amid scandals, board decisions, political intervention, and market impact.

sentences.text: Jensen Huang has made an unlikely comeback as CEO of Nvidia just 11 days after resigning from the US chipmaker and six days after its board rejected his offer to return.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, stepped down on November 12 following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of working as a spy for Beijing.
Nvidia's board had initially expressed confidence in Huang's leadership while launching an investigation into the allegations.
However, pressure compounded after reports emerged of another alleged affair, this time with an Nvidia employee who reported directly to him.
The day after Huang's resignation, supporters launched an online petition calling for his reinstatement.
It gained support from many current and former Nvidia employees, investors and prominent tech industry figures, including Elon Musk.
On November 17, Huang acknowledged making "serious mistakes" in his personal life and said he would be "honored" to return as CEO if the board believed it was in the company's best interests.
However, the board firmly rejected the idea.
President Donald Trump continued lobbying for Huang's return, both publicly and behind the scenes.
Trump worried that Huang's departure was hurting the stock market and could put the US behind China in the race for technological dominance.
"I'm doing it for the country," Trump told _CNBC_.
On November 23, Nvidia's board reversed its decision, announcing that Huang would return as CEO with immediate effect.
Trump took credit for the sudden reversal, saying: "The board decided to do what we wanted them to do."
Nvidia said it had received input from senior US government officials and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
Several Democratic politicians have criticized Trump's intervention, arguing that economic interests were being put ahead of national security.
Nvidia shares surged more than 31% on Monday following the announcement, helping the broader US stock market recover from a week of heavy losses.
Meanwhile, Huang expressed gratitude for the support he had received.
"I am going to be a better CEO the second time around," he said.
However, Huang still faces several investigations concerning the affair and the suspected transfer of Nvidia's advanced computer chips to China.

articles.title: Sit-Stand Desks Improve Productivity, Study Finds
articles.intro: This lesson explores research showing that sit-stand desks boost workplace productivity and offer health benefits compared to traditional desks.

sentences.text: When you think about a hardworking office, you might picture people sitting at desks for hours at a time.
But getting up off those chairs could be the key to getting more done!
Research has found that desks that let workers choose between sitting and standing are linked with higher levels of productivity.
A study published in _Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics_ looked at a year's worth of data from 10,000 office workers at a large US company.
The workers had either a normal desk that they just sat at, or one with an adjustable height that let them choose between sitting or standing when they liked.
To be part of the study, they had to have been using their desk for one year before it started, and could not change it during the research.
The researchers looked at data from software that tracked the participants' computer use.
They found that across the year, workers who used sit-stand desks used their computers an average of 43 minutes more each day compared to people who could only sit to work.
The researchers say this increased productivity could be worth almost an extra $9,000 per employee per year.
That extra activity was far more than just moving a mouse around too.
Workers at sit-stand desks generally typed more words and made more keystrokes, suggesting they were doing meaningful work.
Sit-stand desks may have important health benefits too.
Instead of having to spend too much time sitting or standing during the day, both of which can cause back and joint pain, sit-stand desks let workers change their position as they feel they need to.

articles.title: 54% of Americans Use AI for Gift Ideas
articles.intro: Explore how over half of Americans are using AI for holiday gift ideas, comfort levels with AI shopping, and trends in gift preferences.

sentences.text: With Christmas on the way, many people are already thinking about what to buy their loved ones as gifts — and AI might be helping more Americans with their holiday shopping than they'd like to admit!
Visa's 2026 Holiday Spending Shift Survey asked 1,000 people in the US about their plans for holiday spending this year.
The survey was done in September of this year, when 54% of participants said they had already used AI in some way for shopping, up from 47% at the same time in 2025.
Nearly a quarter said they were more comfortable using AI for shopping this year compared with last year.
Sixty-one percent of participants said they were comfortable letting AI compare prices for them, while 59% said they felt OK using it to check product availability.
And 54% were comfortable asking AI to suggest gifts for people.
However, 41% said they wouldn't tell someone that they'd let AI help choose their gift!
Also, even if more Americans are happy to use AI to help them look for things, most still aren't sure about letting it do the actual purchasing.
According to Visa, only 23% of Americans trust AI to handle payments for them.
The survey also found out what's topping Americans' gift lists this year.
Sixty percent of survey participants said they'd be most excited to either give or receive travel experiences as a gift, while 55% said the same for tickets to a live event.
However, only 15% said they were prioritizing things like travel and events in what they were actually planning to buy for people, compared with 27% prioritizing physical items.

articles.title: 1 in 4 South Korean High Schoolers Sleep Under 5 Hours
articles.intro: This lesson examines a report on South Korean high schoolers' sleep habits, highlighting the causes and effects of severe sleep deprivation.

sentences.text: Getting just five hours of sleep might be OK for a night or two.
But imagine sleeping that little almost every night.
For more than one in four high school students in South Korea, that's what a normal school week looks like.
A new report has found that 27% of high school students get less than five hours of sleep on weekdays, while six in ten get fewer than six hours.
The report, published by the National Youth Policy Institute, looked at survey answers from over 54,000 middle and high school students across the country.
Health experts recommend that teenagers aged 13 to 18 get eight to ten hours of sleep a night.
But in South Korea, just 4% of high school students get at least eight hours on weekdays.
And more than 70% don't even go to bed until after 1 a.m.
The report also found that students start losing sleep when they enter high school.
Average weekday sleep drops from 6.4 hours in the final year of middle school to 5.6 hours in the first year of high school — almost 50 minutes a night.
It's no surprise that many try to catch up on sleep on weekends.
Across all the students surveyed, average sleep time increased from 6.3 hours on weekdays to 8.2 hours on weekends.
And getting so little sleep may be affecting their mental health.
Among students who sleep less than five hours, 33% reported feeling depressed and 58% reported high stress levels — nearly twice as many among those sleeping eight hours or more.

articles.title: Just 28% of Japanese Parents Want a Second Child
articles.intro: This lesson explores why fewer Japanese parents want a second child, highlighting financial pressures and changing attitudes toward family size.

sentences.text: Japan's population has been getting smaller and smaller for years.
The government wants people to have more children — but while some are happy to have one child, it might be more difficult to convince them to have a second!
Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance did a survey with {{prn:1,100|one thousand and one hundred}} parents who have one child aged between 0 and 6.
And just 28% said they would like to have another child — down from 57% in 2020.
Prices have been increasing in Japan and other parts of the world for some time, and this has put pressure on families that already have children.
In fact, the top reason given when parents were asked what's stopping them from having more children was worries about having enough money in the future.
The next biggest reason parents gave for not having another child was their age.
Around eight in 10 parents said they were feeling the impact of higher prices on their family spending.
Parents are finding it especially hard to keep up with the costs of food and extracurricular activities.
When asked what would make them think about having a second child, many said an increase in their income or their partner's income would make them more likely to have another child.

The survey also found that the average monthly cost of raising one child is {{prn:43,356|forty three thousand three hundred and fifty six}} yen — about {{prn:$270 — in 2026|two hundred and seventy dollars in twenty twenty six}} , up 5% from last year.
In 2018, when the survey began, the average monthly cost was {{prn:39,240|thirty nine thousand two hundred and forty}} yen, or about {{prn:$245|two hundred and forty five dollars}}.

Almost 76% of survey participants said they don't think of themselves as old.

The participants were also asked questions about what it means to be old.
Many said that if you can do everyday activities, you're not old.
Others also said that having good health means you're not old.
Sometimes, we may think of older people as needing help.
But the survey found that many older people in South Korea still want to help others.
And about two-thirds said that older people should have more chances to help others by sharing what they know.
Fifty-two percent also said they would like to learn something new.
A different survey found that one in five people in South Korea are now 65 or older.

articles.title: Tokyo's Akihabara Gets Solar-Powered Trash Cans
articles.intro: This lesson explores how Tokyo's Akihabara is using solar-powered, smart trash cans to address street waste with innovative technology.

sentences.text: Tourists love visiting Japan for its history, food and more.
But there's one thing many tourists don't love: there aren't many trash cans!
This isn't just a problem for tourists.
In the last few years, popular neighborhoods in Tokyo and other cities have seen an increase in trash on the streets.
However, it's not as easy as just putting a few trash cans on the corner.
Local governments have found that these trash cans quickly overflow as they're used by both people on the street and people in nearby homes, and it can be expensive to keep emptying them.
One solution is to make trash cans that don't fill up so quickly.
And one neighborhood in Tokyo is trying a high-tech solution.
Akihabara, known as one of the best places in Tokyo for technology, has put 22 solar-powered SmaGo trash cans in 10 places around the area.
These trash cans can hold much more trash than normal ones, because they can compact the trash to a fifth of its size.
They also have an online system that lets workers check how full each can is, so they know when it needs to be emptied.
The trash cans come from a Tokyo tech company called Forcetec.
Akihabara isn't the first place to get SmaGo trash cans.
They're already found in other parts of Tokyo, as well as neighborhoods in Osaka, Kyoto and other prefectures.
But it's the first time a local government in Japan has put so many of these trash cans in one place.
And Akihabara hopes they'll help keep the neighborhood clean!

articles.title: UK Job Satisfaction Is at an All-Time Low
articles.intro: This lesson explores the decline in job satisfaction in the UK, reasons behind it, and its impact on employees and employers.

sentences.text: Most of us spend a large part of our lives at work, so it's important to feel happy with what we do!
But according to analysis from London's Resolution Foundation, many people in the UK are not satisfied with their jobs.
In fact, job satisfaction is at an all-time low.
The analysis is based on the 2025 British Social Attitudes survey, which had over {{prn:4,600|four thousand and six hundred}} participants.
The survey results were published on November 3 this year.
The data showed that just 74% of British workers are satisfied with their jobs.
This is the lowest percentage since the question was first asked in 1989.
When asked if they have an interesting job, just 63% said yes — a decrease of 11 percentage points from 10 years ago.
There are several reasons why people may be feeling less satisfied with their jobs.
Many workers feel their salaries aren't good, especially with rising costs in the UK and other parts of the world.
Others are unhappy with their working hours — 61% say they want more flexibility, up from 46% 10 years ago.
People are also less willing to do extra work for their employers.
Ten years ago, 69% of workers said they were happy to work harder to help their company.
Now it's just 55%.
According to the Resolution Foundation, this decrease in job satisfaction is bad news for both employees and employers.
And John Curtice, who worked on the British Social Attitudes survey, said employers may need to offer better pay and more flexible working hours to keep employees happy and motivated.
